_about: Built from ENTRIES.md by build-bestiary.py; edit the table, not this file. Every entry is proposed unless status is 'Rex'. Labels are JOURNAL.md's eight.

entries.name: The Kraken
entries.section: A. Rex's named items
entries.period_or_tradition: Norse and Scandinavian sailor lore; first full description Pontoppidan 1752, older tales behind it; the real animal behind it is the giant squid (*Architeuthis*)
entries.home: its lair: an underwater dungeon or a sea lane (open)
entries.source: MAGNUS. Hooks (proposed): harpoons and the ship's guns for the arms; a severed arm regrows between phases; whale oil or a bait cask lures it to one side of the ship

entries.name: Opía (hupia), spirit of the dead
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Taíno (Pané c. 1498): the dead leave Coaybay at night to eat guava and lie with the living; told from the living by having no navel
entries.home: guava groves and old cemetery grounds at night; bats are their form
entries.source: PANE. Hook: check the navel (a Perception test) before trusting a stranger at night; bats in the trees are the tell

entries.name: Maquetaurie Guayaba, lord of Coaybay
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Taíno (Pané): lord of the house of the dead
entries.home: Coaybay, a dungeon under an island (a cave)
entries.source: PANE. A ruler of the dead who may be bargained with, like Baron Samedi

entries.name: Guabancex, lady of the hurricane
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Taíno: the goddess of the storm; the word *huracán* comes from this tradition
entries.home: the open sea in hurricane season (ECOLOGY §5: August to October)
entries.source: PANE; Taíno zemí studies. Fought through her heralds; appeased with offerings (open)

entries.name: Guataubá, herald of thunder
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Taíno: Guabancex's herald who announces the storm
entries.source: PANE

entries.name: Coatrisquie, herald of the flood
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Taíno: Guabancex's herald who releases the waters
entries.home: flooded river mouths after a storm
entries.source: PANE

entries.name: Yúcahu, lord of cassava and the sea
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Taíno: the supreme zemí, son of Atabey
entries.home: a zemí stone in a cave shrine
entries.source: PANE. Not an enemy: a shrine that grants or withholds

entries.name: Atabey, mother of waters
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Taíno: goddess of fresh water, fertility and the moon
entries.source: PANE

entries.name: Boinayel and Márohu, the rain twins
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Taíno: the twins who bring and withhold rain
entries.source: PANE

entries.name: A zemí guardian
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Taíno zemí figures (real objects); their waking is this world's own
entries.source: PANE (the objects). Our invention that they move: marked as two labels

entries.name: Ciguapa
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Dominican folklore (Hispaniola), first written 1866; a wild woman with backward feet and hair to the ground who lures men
entries.home: mountain forest; river banks at night
entries.source: FOLK. Her tracks lead the wrong way (a tracking puzzle); caught only on a full-moon night with a black-and-white dog (folk rule)

entries.name: Biembienes
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Dominican folklore: small wild forest people of the Bahoruco, descendants of maroons in the tale
entries.source: FOLK. Open: whether this one is used at all, since the legend is tied to maroon history

entries.name: Galipote
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Dominican folklore: a sorcerer who turns into an animal; immune to blades, hurt by prayer or a blessed weapon
entries.source: FOLK

entries.name: Bacá
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Dominican and Haitian folklore: a familiar demon bought from a sorcerer to guard property, paid in the owner's kin
entries.source: FOLK. A story hook: the bigwig's warehouse (town keeper's; not placed here)

entries.name: Güije (jigüe)
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Cuban folklore: a small black river imp with long hair that drags bathers under
entries.source: FOLK

entries.name: Madre de Aguas
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Cuban folklore: a giant water serpent, thick as a palm, that guards a river or spring
entries.home: a Cuban river mouth; a settlement's water
entries.source: FOLK. Killing it dries the water (balance question)

entries.name: Chupacabra
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Puerto Rican folklore first reported 1995; a goat-sucker
entries.home: goat pens on dry islands at night
entries.source: FOLK. Out-of-period folklore: BESTIARY.md open item 4

entries.name: Garadiablo
entries.section: B. Taíno (Greater Antilles: Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Puerto Rican folklore: a swamp monster of Punta Santiago
entries.source: FOLK

entries.name: Maboya (Mabouya)
entries.section: C. Kalinago (Carib) and the mainland Caribs (Lesser Antilles, Guianas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Kalinago belief (Rochefort 1658, Breton 1665): the evil spirit who sends sickness, storms and eclipses; appeased, not worshipped
entries.source: ROCHEFORT. Hook: the bohique (shaman) or an offering; the sick crew mate's fever is its face

entries.name: Kanaima
entries.section: C. Kalinago (Carib) and the mainland Caribs (Lesser Antilles, Guianas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Carib and Pemon peoples of the Guianas: a ritual killer who stalks a victim for days and must taste the corpse
entries.home: the Guiana coast and rivers; follows the party over the world map
entries.source: FOLK (ethnographies of the Guianas). The hunter role's exemplar

entries.name: Water Mama (Watramama)
entries.section: C. Kalinago (Carib) and the mainland Caribs (Lesser Antilles, Guianas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Guyanese and Surinamese folklore (Arawak and African roots): a river mermaid with a golden comb who drowns the greedy
entries.source: FOLK. Shares the comb motif with River Mumma and Mama Dlo

entries.name: Massacooramaan
entries.section: C. Kalinago (Carib) and the mainland Caribs (Lesser Antilles, Guianas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Guyanese folklore: a huge hairy man-beast that upsets boats on the rivers and eats the crew
entries.source: FOLK

entries.name: Baccoo
entries.section: C. Kalinago (Carib) and the mainland Caribs (Lesser Antilles, Guianas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Guyanese folklore: a short imp kept in a bottle, fed bananas and milk, that throws stones and grants wealth
entries.source: FOLK. A thing you steal or free rather than kill

entries.name: Zombi
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou folk belief: the dead raised and bound to work by a bokor; salt frees them. Written accounts from Moreau de Saint-Méry 1797 onward
entries.home: a bokor's plantation; raised in a fight
entries.faction: free-pirates (Rex: the free pirates give voodoo zombies, COMBAT §4e)
entries.status_detail: proposed (the enemy); Rex (the zombie as a crew mate's resurrection form)
entries.source: MOREAU. Hook: salt on the tongue ends the binding (a non-lethal win)

entries.name: Bokor
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou: a sorcerer who serves the lwa "with both hands"
entries.home: a hounfour at the edge of a town
entries.source: MOREAU

entries.name: Lougawou
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian folklore: a shapeshifting witch who flies as a fireball and drinks children's blood (Moreau 1797 records loup-garou belief in Saint-Domingue)
entries.source: MOREAU. Cousin of the soucouyant

entries.name: Baron Samedi
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou: lwa of the dead and the cemetery; top hat, rum, obscenity
entries.home: the crossroads of the dead; the cemetery gate
entries.source: Vodou tradition. A bargain, never a fight; a plausible gate for the ghost resurrection (story keeper's)

entries.name: Maman Brigitte
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou: Baron Samedi's consort, guardian of the first grave
entries.home: the first grave of any cemetery
entries.source: Vodou tradition

entries.name: Papa Legba
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou: the gatekeeper lwa; opens the way
entries.source: Vodou tradition. The journal's "ask before you pass" being

entries.name: Agwé
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou: lwa of the sea and of sailors; offerings floated on a raft
entries.source: Vodou tradition

entries.name: La Sirène
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou: the mermaid lwa, Agwé's consort, a trumpet and a mirror
entries.source: Vodou tradition. The Merfolk faction's natural figurehead

entries.name: Simbi
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou: water-serpent lwa of springs and rain
entries.source: Vodou tradition

entries.name: Damballa
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou: the great serpent lwa, the sky father
entries.source: Vodou tradition

entries.name: Marinette
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Haitian Vodou: a fierce Petwo lwa; folk tie her to the loup-garou
entries.source: Vodou tradition. Open: whether any Petwo lwa may be an antagonist

entries.name: Yemayá
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Afro-Cuban Santería (Yoruba root: Yemoja): mother of the sea
entries.source: Santería tradition

entries.name: Olokun
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Yoruba and Afro-Cuban tradition: ruler of the deep ocean, chained at the bottom
entries.faction: abyssal-cult (open: a sleeping deep power the cult misreads)
entries.source: Yoruba tradition. Open: whether to let the Abyssal Cult's "ancient oceanic force" echo a real deity at all; the keeper advises against conflating them

entries.name: A nganga's spirit
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Afro-Cuban Palo Monte: the spirit bound in a palero's cauldron
entries.source: Palo tradition

entries.name: Duppy
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Jamaican folklore (Sloane 1707 and Long 1774 record the belief): the shadow of the dead that rises nine nights after death
entries.home: cottonwood trees, graveyards, the town at night
entries.source: SLOANE. Hooks: a Bible, iron, salt; it counts things; call its name backwards

entries.name: Rolling Calf
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Jamaican folklore: a bull-calf duppy with fire eyes dragging a clanking chain; the ghost of a butcher or a wicked man
entries.source: FOLK. Hooks: whistling draws it; a tarred whip or a left-handed knife; a crossroads stops it. (Town note: a butcher's ghost fits the butcher-shop locale; told to the town keeper, not placed here)

entries.name: Ol' Higue
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Jamaican and Guyanese folklore: an old woman who sheds her skin, flies as a fireball and sucks blood
entries.home: a hut at the edge of town
entries.source: FOLK. Hooks: salt the shed skin; spill rice she must count

entries.name: River Mumma
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Jamaican folklore: the river mother with a golden comb; the fish are her children; never fish her pool
entries.source: FOLK. Hook: taking the comb curses; returning it blesses

entries.name: Three-foot Horse
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Jamaican folklore: a three-legged duppy horse that runs down travellers but cannot enter shade
entries.source: FOLK. Hook: stand in a tree's shadow

entries.name: Whooping Boy
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Jamaican folklore: a whooping ghost boy who rides the three-foot horse
entries.source: FOLK

entries.name: Obeah practitioner
entries.section: D. Afro-Caribbean: Haitian Vodou, Afro-Cuban Santería and Palo, Jamaican obeah
entries.period_or_tradition: Jamaican obeah, recorded by Sloane 1707 and prosecuted from 1760; a real practice, its spells folklore
entries.source: SLOANE. The person is historical, the effects folklore: two labels

entries.name: Soucouyant
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Trinidadian and Eastern Caribbean folklore (French Antillean roots: *soukougnan*): an old woman who sheds her skin at night and flies as a ball of fire to drink blood
entries.home: a hut; the night sky over a town
entries.source: FOLK. Hooks: salt or hot pepper in the skin; rice at the crossroads she must count till dawn; she is killed by the sun if kept from her skin

entries.name: La Diablesse
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Trinidadian and St Lucian folklore: a beautiful woman in a wide hat with one cow's hoof who leads men off cliffs
entries.home: forest paths and fêtes at night
entries.source: FOLK. Hooks: turn your clothes inside out; look for the hoof (Perception)

entries.name: Douen
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Trinidadian folklore: the spirits of unbaptised children, faceless under straw hats, feet turned backwards; they call children into the forest by name
entries.source: FOLK. Hooks: never answer your name called from the forest; a shoe sole-up

entries.name: Lagahoo (Ligahoo)
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Trinidadian folklore (French *loup-garou*): a shapeshifter dragging a coffin and chains at midnight
entries.source: FOLK. Hook: beaten with a blessed stick nine days running (a questline, not a fight)

entries.name: Papa Bois
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Trinidadian folklore: the father of the forest, protector of its animals; punishes the greedy hunter
entries.source: FOLK. Hook: a rum offering; he may turn a hunter into a beast (a transformation hook for COMBAT §4e, story keeper's)

entries.name: Mama D'Leau (Mama Dlo)
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Trinidadian folklore: mother of the water, a woman with an anaconda's body; Papa Bois's companion; punishes polluters
entries.source: FOLK. Hook: take off a shoe, turn it over and walk away backwards

entries.name: Moko Jumbie
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Trinidadian and West African tradition: the stilt-walking spirit guardian who sees evil coming
entries.source: FOLK. A protector, not an enemy; could guard a town against duppies

entries.name: Jumbee
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Eastern Caribbean umbrella word for a malevolent spirit of the dead (Barbados, Guyana, the Virgin Islands, Antigua)
entries.home: silk-cotton trees, the beach at night
entries.source: FOLK. Hooks: a pile of sand or rice to count; cross a stream; shoes at the door

entries.name: Heartman
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Barbadian folklore: a man who cuts out children's hearts for the devil
entries.source: FOLK

entries.name: Steel Donkey
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Barbadian folklore: a clanking iron-shod spectral donkey that rides the roads at night
entries.source: FOLK

entries.name: Chickcharney
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Bahamian folklore (Andros): a three-toed owl-like creature with red eyes that nests by tying pine tops together; curses those who mock it, blesses the kind. Its real root may be the extinct giant barn owl *Tyto pollens*
entries.source: FOLK. Pairs with the Prehistoric owl below for the journal's educational side

entries.name: Lusca
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Bahamian folklore: the half-shark half-octopus of the blue holes whose breathing is the tide
entries.source: FOLK. The blue hole breathes: the fight's water level changes on a timer

entries.name: The devils of Bermuda
entries.section: E. Eastern Caribbean folklore (Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, the Windwards, the Bahamas)
entries.period_or_tradition: Spanish sailors called Bermuda the Isle of Devils for the night shrieks: the cahow (Bermuda petrel) and feral hogs, recorded by the Sea Venture survivors 1609
entries.source: Strachey 1610. A journal reveal: the "devils" identify as birds (Historical)

entries.name: Davy Jones
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: English sailor lore; first in print Defoe 1726 (Smollett 1751 gives the saucer eyes and three rows of teeth); Davy Jones's Locker is the sea bottom
entries.home: the sea floor; appears in a storm
entries.source: DEFOE

entries.name: The Flying Dutchman
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Dutch and English sailor lore, written from 1790 (Barrington) with older tellings; a ghost ship that can never make port
entries.source: sailor lore. The Ghost Fleet's flagship or rival (open)

entries.name: Drowned sailor
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: sailor lore of the drowned who return; the Ghost Fleet's green spectres are this world's own (ALIGNMENT §10)
entries.source: sailor lore; the fleet is Rex's faction, its soldiers proposed

entries.name: Mother Carey's chickens
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: storm petrels, which sailors held to be the souls of drowned sailors and heralds of storms; "Mother Carey" is *Mater Cara*
entries.home: the open sea before a storm
entries.source: sailor lore. A journal entry that is a real bird with a folk meaning

entries.name: St Elmo's fire
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: the corona discharge on masts in a storm, taken by sailors as a saint's protection
entries.source: sailor lore. A phenomenon entry (JOURNAL kind: phenomenon), not a creature; listed so the journal has it

entries.name: Sea serpent
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Scandinavian sailor lore and natural history: Olaus Magnus 1555; Hans Egede's 1734 sighting off Greenland
entries.source: MAGNUS

entries.name: Sea monk
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Renaissance natural history: a fish shaped like a monk caught off Denmark 1546 (Rondelet, Belon); likely a squid or angelshark
entries.source: MAGNUS. Candidate "fish person" with a period pedigree

entries.name: Columbus's mermaids
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Columbus's journal, 9 January 1493: three mermaids off Hispaniola, "not as beautiful as painted"; they were manatees
entries.source: COLUMBUS. The journal's model entry: encountered as a mermaid, identified as a manatee

entries.name: Siren
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Greek: the singers whose song wrecks ships (Homer, *Odyssey* XII); bird-women in the old telling, fish-tailed later
entries.home: a siren's rock in a strait
entries.source: Greek tradition. Hook: wax in the ears (Hearing Fe drops to zero, so does the charm); a crew mate lashed to the mast

entries.name: Triton
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Greek: Poseidon's son, the conch-blowing merman; the "tritons" are his kind
entries.source: Greek tradition. Rex's sub-label for the faction: "Tritons / Sirens"

entries.name: Scylla
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Greek: the six-headed monster of the strait (*Odyssey* XII)
entries.source: Greek tradition

entries.name: Charybdis
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Greek: the whirlpool that swallows the sea thrice a day
entries.source: Greek tradition. An environment hazard, not a unit

entries.name: Hippocampus
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Greek: the fish-tailed horse of Poseidon's chariot
entries.source: Greek tradition

entries.name: Atlantean warden
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Atlantis is Plato's (*Timaeus*, *Critias*, c. 360 BC); the Machina are Rex's faction's sci-fi
entries.home: a sunken Atlantean site (an underwater dungeon)
entries.source: Plato; the faction is Rex's (ALIGNMENT §10)

entries.name: Leviathan
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Hebrew Bible (Job 41, Psalm 74, Isaiah 27): the sea monster of the deep
entries.source: Hebrew tradition

entries.name: The great fish
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Hebrew Bible (Jonah 1–2): the fish that swallows a man for three days
entries.source: Hebrew tradition. A swallowed-whole set piece inside a boss (kraken or leviathan) is an alternative use

entries.name: Hy-Brasil
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Irish legend; on charts from 1325 to 1865, an island seen one day in seven
entries.home: west of Ireland; here, an Atlantic minor locale
entries.source: charts. A place entry for the journal (kind: place); the town keeper's if it becomes a locale

entries.name: Antillia, Isle of Seven Cities
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: Iberian legend of seven bishops who fled the Moors in 714; on the 1424 Pizzigano chart; gave the Antilles their name
entries.source: charts. As Hy-Brasil

entries.name: The Fountain of Youth
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: the Bimini legend attached to Ponce de León (Oviedo 1535; Ponce's 1513 contract never names it)
entries.source: Oviedo. A place and an item, not a creature; listed for the journal

entries.name: El Dorado
entries.section: F. European sailor lore and classical myth
entries.period_or_tradition: the gilded man of the Muisca, pursued by Raleigh in Guiana (1595)
entries.home: the Guiana interior; a minor locale
entries.source: Raleigh 1596

entries.name: Lost Boy
entries.section: G. Fiction the factions draw on (Fantasy, with author and year)
entries.period_or_tradition: J. M. Barrie, *Peter Pan* (1904 play, 1911 novel)
entries.source: BARRIE. Rex's faction name is "Lost Boys / Peter Pan Pirates"

entries.name: The crocodile that swallowed a clock
